lessons.title: Energy Stores, Transfers and Power
lessons.description: How energy is stored, transferred between stores, and how to calculate power and work done.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Stores

Energy cannot be created or destroyed — it can only be transferred between different energy stores. You need to know eight energy stores.

Key Fact

The eight energy stores are: kinetic, thermal, chemical, elastic potential, gravitational potential, electrostatic, magnetic, and nuclear.

Kinetic energy depends on the mass and speed of an object. The equation is:

$$E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$$

Where \(E_k\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in metres per second (m/s).

Gravitational potential energy depends on the mass, height, and gravitational field strength:

$$E_p = m g h$$

Where \(E_p\) is gravitational potential energy in joules, \(m\) is mass in kg, \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth), and \(h\) is height in metres.

Elastic potential energy is stored when an object is stretched or compressed:

$$E_e = \frac{1}{2} k e^2$$

Where \(E_e\) is elastic potential energy in J, \(k\) is the spring constant in N/m, and \(e\) is the extension in metres. This only applies up to the limit of proportionality.

Energy Transfers

Energy moves between stores by four transfer pathways: mechanically (by forces), electrically (by currents), by heating, and by radiation (light, sound, or other waves).

When a ball is thrown upwards, energy transfers from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential store. At the top, the ball momentarily stops — all kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy. As it falls, the transfer reverses.

Key Fact

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can be transferred usefully, stored, or dissipated — but cannot be created or destroyed. The total energy of a closed system always stays the same.

A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m. Calculate the speed just before it hits the ground (assume no air resistance).

Step 1: \(E_p = mgh = 2 \times 10 \times 5 = 100\) J

Step 2: Set \(E_k = E_p\), so \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = 100\)

Step 3: \(v^2 = \frac{2 \times 100}{2} = 100\), so \(v = 10\) m/s

Work Done and Power

When a force moves an object, work done equals the energy transferred:

$$W = F s$$

Where \(W\) is work done in joules, \(F\) is force in newtons (N), and \(s\) is distance along the line of action of the force in metres.

Power is the rate of energy transfer:

$$P = \frac{E}{t} \quad \text{and} \quad P = \frac{W}{t}$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy transferred in joules, and \(t\) is time in seconds. One watt equals one joule per second.

If an object moves at constant speed, you can combine the equations: \(P = Fv\), where \(v\) is speed in m/s. This is useful for calculating the power output of engines or motors.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For calculation questions, always write the equation first, then substitute your values, then give the answer with correct units. If a question says “calculate,” you must use an equation — you will not get marks for just stating the answer. Watch unit conversions: mass in kg, height in metres, speed in m/s.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • There are eight energy stores; energy transfers between them by four pathways (mechanical, electrical, heating, radiation)
  • Key equations: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), \(E_p = mgh\), \(W = Fs\), \(P = E/t\)
  • Energy is always conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or dissipated

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy, Efficiency and Energy Resources
lessons.description: Why energy is always conserved, how to calculate efficiency, and the pros and cons of energy resources.
lessons.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can never be created or destroyed. In any energy transfer, the total energy before and after is always the same.

In a closed system, where nothing can enter or leave, the total energy stays constant. However, in most real-world situations energy is dissipated — it spreads out to the surroundings as thermal energy and becomes increasingly difficult to use.

Key Fact

Energy is never “lost” — when we say energy is wasted, we mean it has been transferred to less useful stores (usually thermal energy in the surroundings). The total energy in the system has not changed.

Efficiency

Efficiency tells you how good a device is at transferring energy to useful stores. It is calculated using:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output energy}}{\text{total input energy}}$$

Efficiency can also be calculated using power:

$$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful output power}}{\text{total input power}}$$

Efficiency is a ratio and has no units. It is always between 0 and 1. To express it as a percentage, multiply by 100. No device can ever be more than 100% efficient.

A motor uses 500 J of electrical energy and transfers 350 J to the kinetic store. Calculate the efficiency.

\(\text{efficiency} = \frac{350}{500} = 0.70\) or 70%

This means 70% of the input energy is usefully transferred. The remaining 30% (150 J) is dissipated as thermal energy due to friction and sound.

Key Fact

Ways to increase efficiency include reducing friction (lubrication, streamlining), using thermal insulation to reduce unwanted heating, and improving design to minimise energy dissipation.

Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfers

Thermal insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating. In a house, loft insulation, cavity wall insulation, and double glazing all reduce the amount of thermal energy lost to the surroundings.

Lubrication reduces friction between moving parts. This means less energy is wasted as heat in the thermal store, so more energy goes to the useful output.

The thicker the walls of a house, the slower the rate of thermal energy transfer. Cavity wall insulation traps air between the inner and outer walls. Since air is a poor conductor, this reduces energy transfer by conduction. Double glazing works on the same principle — a layer of gas between two panes of glass reduces conduction and convection.

Energy Resources

Energy resources can be classified as non-renewable or renewable.

Non-renewable resources include fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) and nuclear fuel. These are finite — once used up, they cannot be replaced within a human timescale.

Renewable resources include solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave power, and biofuels. These are replenished naturally and will not run out.

Fossil fuels are reliable and produce large amounts of energy, but release carbon dioxide (contributing to climate change) and are running out. Nuclear power is reliable and produces no carbon dioxide during operation, but produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years.

Renewable resources produce no greenhouse gases during operation and will not run out. However, many are weather-dependent (solar, wind) or location-dependent (tidal, geothermal), and some have high initial costs or low power output compared to fossil fuels.

The UK is working towards generating more electricity from renewable sources to reduce carbon emissions and meet climate targets. However, a mix of energy resources is needed to ensure a reliable supply.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In efficiency questions, always check whether the answer should be a decimal or a percentage. If the question says “calculate the efficiency,” give a decimal unless it specifically asks for a percentage. When comparing energy resources, use specific advantages and disadvantages — “it is bad for the environment” is too vague. Say “it releases carbon dioxide which contributes to climate change.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Energy is conserved in all transfers — wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings, usually as thermal energy
  • Efficiency = useful output / total input (always between 0 and 1); improved by reducing friction and adding insulation
  • Energy resources are either renewable (replenished naturally) or non-renewable (finite); the UK needs a mix for reliable supply

lessons.title: Circuits: Current, Resistance and Potential Difference
lessons.description: Covers electric current and charge, potential difference, resistance and ohm's law and more.
lessons.content_html:
Electric Current and Charge

Electric current is the flow of charge carriers through a conductor. In metals, these charge carriers are electrons that move through the wire when a voltage is applied.

Key Fact

Current is measured in amperes (A) and represents the amount of charge flowing past a point per second. The equation is \(I = \frac{Q}{t}\) where I is current, Q is charge in coulombs, and t is time in seconds.

Current is measured using an ammeter, which must be connected in series with the component you want to measure. This ensures all the current flows through the ammeter.

Potential Difference

Potential difference (also called voltage) is the driving force that pushes current around a circuit. It represents the energy transferred per coulomb of charge.

The equation for potential difference is:

$$V = \frac{W}{Q}$$

Where V is potential difference in volts, W is work done (energy transferred) in joules, and Q is charge in coulombs.

Potential difference is measured using a voltmeter. Unlike an ammeter, a voltmeter must be connected in parallel with the component. This allows it to measure the energy difference between the two points without affecting the current flow.

Think of potential difference like the height difference in a waterfall — the greater the height difference, the more energy each drop of water has when it reaches the bottom.

Resistance and Ohm's Law

Resistance opposes the flow of current in a circuit. Different materials and components have different resistances — metals have low resistance while insulators have very high resistance.

Key Fact

Ohm's Law states that \(V = I \times R\) where V is potential difference in volts, I is current in amperes, and R is resistance in ohms (Ω). This relationship only applies to ohmic conductors at constant temperature.

You can rearrange Ohm's law to find any of the three quantities:

$$I = \frac{V}{R} \text{ and } R = \frac{V}{I}$$

The resistance of a wire depends on four factors: its length (longer = higher resistance), cross-sectional area (thicker = lower resistance), material (different metals have different resistivity), and temperature (higher temperature usually = higher resistance for metals).

Some components like filament bulbs are non-ohmic — their resistance changes with temperature, so they don't follow Ohm's law exactly.

Series Circuits

In a series circuit, components are connected end-to-end in a single loop. Current has only one path to follow.

Key Fact

In series circuits: current is the same everywhere (\(I_1 = I_2 = I_3\)), potential difference is shared between components (\(V_{total} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\)), and total resistance equals the sum of individual resistances (\(R_{total} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\)).

If one component fails in a series circuit, the whole circuit stops working because the current path is broken. This is why old Christmas lights used to all go out when one bulb failed.

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, components are connected on separate branches. Current can follow multiple paths.

In parallel circuits, each component receives the full supply voltage. This is why household appliances are connected in parallel — each device gets the full 230V regardless of what other appliances are switched on.

In parallel circuits: potential difference is the same across each branch (\(V_1 = V_2 = V_3\)), total current equals the sum of branch currents (\(I_{total} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\)), and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

The formula for total resistance in parallel is: \(\frac{1}{R_{total}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}\)

Electrical Power

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer in a circuit. It tells us how quickly electrical energy is being converted to other forms like heat, light or motion.

The basic power equation is:

$$P = V \times I$$

Where P is power in watts, V is potential difference in volts, and I is current in amperes. By combining this with Ohm's law, we get two more useful equations: \(P = I^2R\) and \(P = \frac{V^2}{R}\).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When drawing circuit diagrams, always use the correct symbols and show ammeters in series, voltmeters in parallel. For calculations, identify what you're given and what you need to find, then choose the appropriate equation. Remember that in series circuits everything adds up (V and R), but in parallel circuits only current adds up.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Current is the flow of charge (\(I = Q/t\)), potential difference is energy per charge (\(V = W/Q\)), and they're related by Ohm's law (\(V = IR\))
  • In series circuits: same current everywhere, voltages add up, resistances add up
  • In parallel circuits: same voltage on each branch, currents add up, total resistance is less than any individual resistance

lessons.title: Series and Parallel Circuits
lessons.description: Rules for current, voltage and resistance in series and parallel circuits, plus I-V characteristics.
lessons.content_html:
Series Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are connected in a single loop. There is only one path for current to flow, so the current is the same at every point in the circuit.

Key Fact

In a series circuit: current is the same everywhere, potential differences add up to equal the supply voltage, and total resistance equals the sum of all individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\).

The potential difference is shared between components in series. The larger the resistance of a component, the greater its share of the total voltage. If two identical resistors are in series, each gets half the supply voltage.

A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor. Calculate the current and the voltage across each resistor.

Step 1: Total resistance \(R_{\text{total}} = 4 + 8 = 12 \; \Omega\)

Step 2: Current \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1\) A (same throughout)

Step 3: \(V_1 = IR_1 = 1 \times 4 = 4\) V across the 4 Ω resistor

Step 4: \(V_2 = IR_2 = 1 \times 8 = 8\) V across the 8 Ω resistor

Check: \(4 + 8 = 12\) V, which equals the supply voltage.

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, components are connected on separate branches. Each branch provides a different path for the current to flow through.

Key Fact

In a parallel circuit: potential difference is the same across each branch, currents in the branches add up to give the total current from the supply, and total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

The total resistance of resistors in parallel is found using:

$$\frac{1}{R_{\text{total}}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}$$

Adding more resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance, because there are more paths for the current. This means the total current from the battery increases.

Two resistors (6 Ω and 3 Ω) are connected in parallel across a 12 V supply. Calculate the current in each branch and the total current.

Branch 1: \(I_1 = \frac{V}{R_1} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) A

Branch 2: \(I_2 = \frac{V}{R_2} = \frac{12}{3} = 4\) A

Total current: \(I_{\text{total}} = 2 + 4 = 6\) A

Investigating Components

You need to know the I-V characteristics of three components: fixed resistors (ohmic conductors), filament lamps, and diodes.

A fixed resistor gives a straight line through the origin on an I-V graph — current is directly proportional to voltage (Ohm’s law). A filament lamp gives a curve: as current increases, the wire heats up and resistance increases. A diode only conducts in one direction — it has very high resistance in reverse bias.

To investigate the I-V characteristics of a component, connect it in series with a variable resistor, ammeter, and power supply. Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the component. Vary the resistance using the variable resistor to change the current and voltage. Record pairs of I and V values, then swap the power supply connections to get negative values. Plot V on the x-axis and I on the y-axis.

Two other important components are the thermistor and the LDR (light-dependent resistor). A thermistor’s resistance drops as temperature rises, making it useful in temperature sensors. An LDR’s resistance drops as light intensity increases, making it useful in automatic lighting circuits.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam mistake is mixing up series and parallel rules. Remember: in series, current is the same everywhere and voltages add up; in parallel, voltage is the same across branches and currents add up. When asked to “describe” I-V characteristics, refer to the shape of the graph and what happens to resistance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Series: same current, voltages add up, \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2\); Parallel: same voltage, currents add up, \(\frac{1}{R_T} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2}\)
  • I-V graphs: resistors give straight lines, filament lamps curve, diodes only conduct in one direction
  • Thermistor resistance decreases with temperature; LDR resistance decreases with light intensity

lessons.title: Domestic Electricity, Power and the National Grid
lessons.description: Mains electricity, plug wiring and safety, power equations, and how the National Grid works.
lessons.content_html:
Domestic Electricity

The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. This means the current changes direction 50 times per second. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.), which always flows in the same direction.

Key Fact

UK mains supply: alternating current (a.c.), approximately 230 V, frequency 50 Hz. Batteries supply direct current (d.c.).

The Three-Pin Plug

Most appliances connect to the mains via a three-pin plug. The three wires are:

Live wire (brown) — carries the alternating potential difference from the supply. It alternates between about +325 V and −325 V.

Neutral wire (blue) — completes the circuit. It is at, or close to, 0 V (earth potential).

Earth wire (green and yellow) — a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. It carries current to earth if a fault occurs, preventing electric shock.

The live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off, because it is still at 230 V relative to earth. If you touch it, a large potential difference exists between you and the ground, causing a current to flow through your body. This can cause serious injury or death. A switch is always connected in the live wire so that when it is off, no current can reach the appliance.

Key Fact

The fuse is connected in the live wire. If too much current flows (due to a fault), the fuse wire melts, breaking the circuit and preventing overheating or fire. A circuit breaker does the same job but can be reset instead of replaced.

Electrical Power and Energy Transfer

The power of an appliance tells you how much energy it transfers per second. Two equations link power to current and voltage:

$$P = IV$$

$$P = I^2 R$$

Where \(P\) is power in watts, \(I\) is current in amps, \(V\) is potential difference in volts, and \(R\) is resistance in ohms.

The energy transferred by an appliance depends on its power and how long it is used:

$$E = Pt$$

Where \(E\) is energy in joules, \(P\) is power in watts, and \(t\) is time in seconds. You can also use \(E = QV\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs.

A 2 kW kettle is used for 3 minutes. Calculate the energy transferred in joules and in kilowatt-hours.

In joules: \(E = Pt = 2000 \times 180 = 360{,}000\) J

In kWh: \(E = 2 \times \frac{3}{60} = 0.1\) kWh. If electricity costs 30p per kWh, the cost is \(0.1 \times 30 = 3\)p.

The National Grid

The National Grid is a network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to homes and businesses across the UK.

Electricity is transmitted at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V) and low currents. Since power lost as heat in the cables equals \(P = I^2 R\), reducing the current dramatically reduces the energy wasted.

Transformers change the voltage of an a.c. supply. A step-up transformer increases the voltage at the power station before transmission. A step-down transformer decreases the voltage near homes to a safe 230 V.

When voltage is increased, current decreases (assuming power stays the same: \(P = IV\)). This is why high-voltage transmission wastes less energy — the lower current means less heating in the cables.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about the National Grid often ask you to explain why high voltage is used for transmission. Always name the type of transformer (step-up at the power station, step-down near homes).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK mains is a.c. at 230 V, 50 Hz; the live wire is dangerous even when the switch is off
  • Power equations: \(P = IV\), \(P = I^2R\); energy transferred: \(E = Pt\)
  • The National Grid uses high voltage and low current to reduce energy losses in transmission cables

lessons.title: Density, States of Matter and Changes of State
lessons.description: Covers what is density?, the three states of matter, changes of state and more.
lessons.content_html:
What is Density?

Density is a measure of how much mass is packed into a given volume. Every material has its own characteristic density, which helps us identify different substances and predict whether they will float or sink.

Key Fact

Density is calculated using the equation: \(\text{density} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{volume}}\) or \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\)

The unit for density is kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m³), though you might also see grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³). To convert between these units, remember that 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

A block of wood has a mass of 800 g and a volume of 1000 cm³. Its density is:

$$\rho = \frac{800\text{ g}}{1000\text{ cm}^3} = 0.8\text{ g/cm}^3$$

Since this is less than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³), the wood will float.

The Three States of Matter

Matter exists in three main states: solid, liquid, and gas. The differences between these states depend on how the particles are arranged and how they move.

Key Fact

In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions. In liquids, particles can slide past each other. In gases, particles move freely and rapidly in all directions.

Solids

In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern. They are held in place by strong forces of attraction and can only vibrate about their fixed positions. This gives solids their definite shape and volume.

Liquids

In a liquid, particles are still close together but not in a regular arrangement. The forces between particles are weaker than in solids, allowing particles to move past each other. This means liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container.

Gases

In a gas, particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds. The forces between particles are very weak. Gases have no definite shape or volume and will expand to fill any container.

Changes of State

When we heat or cool a substance, we can change its state. These changes are physical changes — the substance itself doesn’t change, only the arrangement and movement of its particles.

There are six possible changes of state:

  • Melting: solid → liquid (heating)
  • Freezing: liquid → solid (cooling)
  • Evaporation/Boiling: liquid → gas (heating)
  • Condensation: gas → liquid (cooling)
  • Sublimation: solid → gas (heating)
  • Deposition: gas → solid (cooling)

Temperature During Changes of State

During a change of state, the temperature remains constant even though we continue to supply energy. This is because the energy is being used to break or form bonds between particles rather than increase their kinetic energy.

Key Fact

The temperature at which a solid melts is called its melting point. The temperature at which a liquid boils is called its boiling point. These are characteristic properties of each substance.

Density Changes During State Changes

When a substance changes state, its density usually changes too. This happens because the particles become more or less tightly packed together, changing the volume while the mass stays the same.

Generally, solids are denser than liquids, which are denser than gases. However, there are important exceptions — ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice floats.

Water is unusual because its solid form (ice) is less dense than its liquid form. When water freezes, the molecules arrange themselves in a hexagonal crystal structure that takes up more space than the liquid arrangement.

Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³ while liquid water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³. This 8% difference is enough to make ice float, which is crucial for life on Earth as it insulates water beneath from freezing completely.

Practical Applications

Understanding density and states of matter has many practical applications. Engineers use density to choose materials for different purposes — aircraft need low-density materials to reduce weight, while ship anchors need high-density materials to sink effectively.

In everyday life, we use changes of state constantly: cooking involves melting butter and boiling water, while refrigeration relies on condensation and evaporation cycles.

Exam Tip

When calculating density, always check your units carefully. Make sure mass is in kg and volume is in m³ for the standard SI unit of kg/m³. Remember that during changes of state, temperature stays constant — this is a common exam question.

Key Takeaways

  • Density equals mass divided by volume and is measured in kg/m³
  • The three states of matter differ in particle arrangement and movement
  • During changes of state, temperature remains constant while energy breaks or forms particle bonds

lessons.title: Internal Energy, Specific Heat Capacity and Latent Heat
lessons.description: Covers what is internal energy?, specific heat capacity, latent heat and changes of state and more.
lessons.content_html:
What is Internal Energy?

All matter is made up of particles that are constantly moving. The internal energy of a substance is the total energy stored by all the particles inside it. This energy comes from two sources:

  • The kinetic energy of particles moving around (vibrating, rotating, or moving freely)
  • The potential energy stored in the forces between particles
Key Fact

Internal energy increases when a substance is heated and decreases when it cools down. The internal energy determines both the temperature and the state of matter.

When you heat a substance, you transfer energy to it. This energy makes the particles move faster and can also change how they’re arranged. The amount of internal energy depends on the substance’s temperature, mass, and what material it’s made from.

Specific Heat Capacity

Different materials need different amounts of energy to heat up by the same amount. For example, water takes much more energy to heat up than copper. This property is called specific heat capacity.

The relationship between energy, mass, temperature change, and specific heat capacity is given by:

$$\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T$$

Where:

  • \(\Delta E\) = change in thermal energy (J)
  • \(m\) = mass (kg)
  • \(c\) = specific heat capacity (J/kg°C)
  • \(\Delta T\) = temperature change (°C)
Key Fact

Water has a very high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg°C), which is why it’s good for heating systems and why coastal areas have milder temperatures than inland areas.

Materials with high specific heat capacity take more energy to heat up but also store more energy when hot. This makes them good thermal stores. Metals generally have lower specific heat capacities than water, which is why a metal spoon heats up quickly in hot soup.

Latent Heat and Changes of State

When you heat ice, something interesting happens. At first, the temperature rises as the ice warms up. But when it reaches 0°C, the temperature stops rising even though you’re still adding energy. Instead, the ice melts into water. This energy is called latent heat.

There are two main types of latent heat:

  • Latent heat of fusion — energy needed to melt a solid or freeze a liquid
  • Latent heat of vaporisation — energy needed to boil a liquid or condense a gas

The latent heat of vaporisation is always much larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance.

During a change of state, all the energy goes into breaking or forming bonds between particles rather than making them move faster. This is why the temperature stays constant during melting, boiling, condensing, or freezing.

The energy required for a change of state is calculated using: \(E = m \times L\), where \(E\) is energy (J), \(m\) is mass (kg), and \(L\) is the specific latent heat (J/kg).

Particle Model Explanation

The particle model helps explain these energy changes. In a solid, particles vibrate in fixed positions with strong forces holding them together. When heated, particles vibrate more vigorously, increasing the temperature.

Solid to liquid (melting): Energy breaks some bonds between particles. They can now slide past each other but stay close together.

Liquid to gas (boiling): Energy completely overcomes forces between particles. They move freely and far apart.

Gas to liquid (condensing): Particles lose energy and forces pull them back together.

Liquid to solid (freezing): Particles lose more energy and lock into fixed positions.

This model explains why gases take up much more space than liquids or solids, and why different substances have different melting and boiling points — it depends on how strong the forces between their particles are.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In calculations, always check your units carefully. Energy should be in joules (J), mass in kilograms (kg), and temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). Remember that during state changes, temperature stays constant even though energy is still being transferred. Practice using both the specific heat capacity equation and the latent heat equation — the exam will test both.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all particles in a substance
  • Specific heat capacity determines how much energy is needed to change temperature: \(\Delta E = m \times c \times \Delta T\)
  • Latent heat is energy needed for state changes without temperature change: \(E = m \times L\)

lessons.title: Atomic Structure, Radioactivity and Half-Life
lessons.description: How the atomic model developed, types of nuclear radiation, and calculating half-life.
lessons.content_html:
The Model of the Atom

Our understanding of atomic structure has developed over time. The first model was the solid sphere model proposed by Dalton in the early 1800s. He imagined atoms as tiny, indivisible balls.

In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model — a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons scattered throughout, like plums in a pudding.

Key Fact

In 1909, Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil. Most passed straight through, but some were deflected and a few bounced back. This proved the atom has a tiny, dense, positive nucleus with electrons orbiting at a distance — the nuclear model.

Bohr refined the nuclear model by proposing that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances in fixed energy levels (shells). Niels Bohr’s model explained why atoms emit and absorb specific frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.

Later, James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing our picture of the atom: a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels.

Radioactive Decay

Some atomic nuclei are radioactive — they are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable. This process is called radioactive decay and is random. You cannot predict when a particular nucleus will decay.

Key Fact

There are three types of nuclear radiation: alpha (\(\alpha\)) particles, beta (\(\beta\)) particles, and gamma (\(\gamma\)) rays. Each has different properties, penetrating power, and ionising ability.

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium nucleus). Strongly ionising, stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. The atomic number decreases by 2 and the mass number decreases by 4.

Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton. Moderately ionising, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. The atomic number increases by 1, mass number stays the same.

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — an electromagnetic wave with no mass or charge. Weakly ionising, only reduced significantly by several centimetres of lead or thick concrete. The atomic number and mass number are unchanged.

Half-Life

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for half the unstable nuclei to decay, or for the count rate (activity) to fall to half its original value.

After one half-life, half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives, a quarter remain. After three half-lives, one-eighth remain, and so on.

A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. After 30 minutes, the activity is 100 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

800 → 400 → 200 → 100 = three half-lives

Three half-lives = 30 minutes, so one half-life = \(\frac{30}{3} = 10\) minutes.

Uses and Hazards of Radiation

Nuclear radiation has useful applications: gamma rays are used in medical tracers and to sterilise equipment; beta radiation is used in thickness gauges; alpha sources are used in smoke detectors.

Contamination occurs when radioactive material gets onto or inside the body. This is more dangerous because the source stays close to cells. Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source — once the source is removed, the exposure stops.

Precautions include: keeping radioactive sources in lead-lined containers, using tongs to handle sources, wearing protective clothing, and minimising exposure time.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Half-life questions often ask you to read values from a graph. Find the starting activity, halve it, and read across to the time axis. If asked for the fraction remaining after several half-lives, remember: each half-life halves what’s left. Know the difference between contamination (material on you) and irradiation (radiation from outside).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The atomic model evolved from solid spheres through plum pudding to the nuclear model after Rutherford’s gold foil experiment
  • Three types of radiation: alpha (helium nucleus, most ionising), beta (electron, moderate), gamma (EM wave, least ionising)
  • Half-life is the time for half the unstable nuclei to decay; contamination is more hazardous than irradiation

lessons.title: Static Electricity and Electric Fields
lessons.description: How objects become charged by friction and the nature of electric fields.
lessons.content_html:
Static Charge and Electron Transfer

All matter is made of atoms, which contain positively charged protons, negatively charged electrons and neutral neutrons. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the overall charge is zero.

When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons are transferred from one surface to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged, while the material that loses electrons becomes positively charged. This is called static electricity.

Key Fact

Only electrons move when objects are charged by friction — protons are fixed in the nucleus and cannot transfer between materials.

For example, when a polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons transfer from the cloth to the rod. The rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth becomes positively charged. If a Perspex rod is rubbed with a cloth, electrons transfer from the rod to the cloth, leaving the rod positively charged.

Attraction, Repulsion and Sparking

Charged objects exert forces on each other without touching. Two objects with the same charge (both positive or both negative) repel each other. Two objects with opposite charges attract each other. A charged object can also attract a neutral object by electrostatic induction — the charge on the nearby object causes electrons in the neutral object to move, creating regions of opposite charge on its surface.

Key Fact

Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. This rule governs all electrostatic interactions.

When a charged object is brought close to an earthed conductor, the potential difference between them can become large enough to ionise the air. Electrons jump across the gap, creating a spark. Lightning is a large-scale example of this — charge builds up in clouds until the potential difference between the cloud and the ground is high enough to cause a massive spark discharge.

Earthing allows charge to flow safely to the ground through a conducting path. This prevents dangerous build-up of static charge. Fuel tankers use earthing straps and aircraft are earthed before refuelling to avoid sparks near flammable fuel.

Electric Fields

A charged object creates an electric field around it. Any other charged object placed in this field will experience a force. The closer to the charged object, the stronger the field — this is shown by field lines drawn closer together.

Electric field lines point away from positive charges and towards negative charges. For a single point charge, the field lines are radial (spreading outwards). Between two parallel charged plates, the field is uniform — the field lines are parallel and equally spaced, meaning the force on a charge is the same everywhere between the plates.

The strength of the electric field depends on the size of the charge producing it and the distance from the charge. A stronger charge creates a stronger field. The field gets weaker as you move further from the charge — this is an example of a non-contact force.

The force between two charged objects also depends on both charges and the distance between them. Doubling the distance between charges significantly reduces the force between them. This relationship is important for understanding how charged particles interact in circuits and in everyday static phenomena.

Uses and Dangers of Static Electricity

Static electricity has practical uses. In electrostatic sprayers, paint or crop spray is given an electric charge so that the droplets repel each other, creating a fine, even mist. The object being sprayed is earthed, so it attracts the charged droplets, reducing waste and giving an even coating — even on the back of the object.

In photocopiers and laser printers, static charge is used to attract toner particles to specific areas of a drum, which are then transferred to paper. Electrostatic precipitators in chimneys use charged plates to remove smoke particles from waste gases before they escape into the atmosphere.

Static electricity can be dangerous in certain situations. When refuelling aircraft or filling fuel tankers, friction between flowing fuel and pipes can build up static charge. A spark near flammable fuel vapour could cause an explosion. This is why earthing straps are used and operators touch metal parts before handling fuel nozzles.

In hospitals, static sparks near oxygen-rich environments or flammable anaesthetics pose a fire risk. Anti-static flooring and clothing help prevent charge build-up. Similarly, electronic components can be damaged by electrostatic discharge, so technicians wear anti-static wrist straps when handling circuit boards.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining charging by friction, always state that electrons transfer (not protons). Identify which material gains and which loses electrons. For electric field questions, remember to draw arrows pointing away from positive charges and towards negative charges, and show field lines closer together where the field is stronger.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Static charge is caused by the transfer of electrons between insulating materials — the material gaining electrons becomes negative, the one losing them becomes positive.
  • Like charges repel, opposite charges attract; charged objects create electric fields that exert non-contact forces on other charges.
  • Electric field lines run from positive to negative; closer lines mean a stronger field; uniform fields exist between parallel plates.

lessons.title: Gas Pressure and Pressure in Fluids
lessons.description: Understanding gas pressure, atmospheric pressure and pressure in liquids.
lessons.content_html:
Gas Pressure and the Particle Model

Gases consist of particles that are in constant random motion. As these particles collide with the walls of their container, they exert a force on the surface. The total force per unit area is the gas pressure. The more frequent or forceful the collisions, the higher the pressure.

Increasing the temperature of a gas gives the particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide with the walls more frequently and with greater force. If the volume of the container is fixed, this increases the pressure. This explains why aerosol cans carry warnings not to heat them — the pressure inside can build up enough to cause an explosion.

Key Fact

For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure and volume are inversely proportional: \(p \times V = \text{constant}\). This is known as Boyle’s Law.

If you compress a gas (reduce its volume), the particles have less space and hit the walls more often, so the pressure increases. If you expand the gas, the particles have more space, collide less often, and the pressure decreases. The relationship is: \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\), where subscripts 1 and 2 refer to the initial and final states.

A gas occupies 0.5 m³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. The gas is compressed to 0.2 m³ at constant temperature. What is the new pressure?

Using \(p_1 V_1 = p_2 V_2\):

$$p_2 = \frac{p_1 V_1}{V_2} = \frac{100 \times 0.5}{0.2} = 250 \text{ kPa}$$

Pressure in Fluids and Atmospheric Pressure

A fluid is any substance that can flow — both liquids and gases are fluids. Pressure acts in all directions within a fluid. The pressure at any point in a fluid depends on the depth, the density of the fluid and gravitational field strength.

The pressure due to a column of liquid is calculated using:

$$p = h \rho g$$

where \(p\) is pressure in pascals (Pa), \(h\) is the height of the liquid column in metres, \(\rho\) is the density of the liquid in kg/m³, and \(g\) is gravitational field strength (9.8 N/kg on Earth).

Key Fact

Pressure in a liquid increases with depth. A diver at 10 m experiences roughly double the atmospheric pressure — one atmosphere from the air above, plus one atmosphere-equivalent from the water.

Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of air molecules above a surface. At sea level, atmospheric pressure is approximately 101,325 Pa (about 101 kPa). As altitude increases, there are fewer air molecules above, so atmospheric pressure decreases. This is why air pressure is lower on top of a mountain than at sea level.

Because pressure increases with depth, the bottom of an object submerged in a fluid experiences a greater pressure than the top. This difference in pressure creates an upward force called upthrust (or buoyancy). If the upthrust equals the weight of the object, it floats. If the weight is greater than the upthrust, the object sinks.

An object floats when it displaces a volume of fluid whose weight equals its own weight. This is why a steel ship floats — its hollow shape displaces a large volume of water, creating enough upthrust to support its weight, even though steel is denser than water.

Pressure Differences and Everyday Examples

Pressure differences cause fluids to flow. When you drink through a straw, you reduce the air pressure inside the straw by expanding your lungs. The higher atmospheric pressure on the surface of the drink pushes the liquid up the straw. Similarly, suction cups work because removing air from inside the cup creates a lower pressure, and atmospheric pressure on the outside holds the cup in place.

Hydraulic systems use the fact that pressure is transmitted equally through an incompressible fluid. A small force applied to a small piston creates a pressure that acts equally on a larger piston, producing a larger force. The relationship is:

$$\frac{F_1}{A_1} = \frac{F_2}{A_2}$$

This principle is used in hydraulic brakes, car jacks and industrial presses.

Calculate the pressure at the bottom of a swimming pool that is 2.5 m deep. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and \(g = 9.8\) N/kg.

Using \(p = h \rho g\):

$$p = 2.5 \times 1000 \times 9.8 = 24{,}500 \text{ Pa} = 24.5 \text{ kPa}$$

This is the pressure from the water alone. The total pressure at the bottom would also include atmospheric pressure (approximately 101 kPa), giving a total of about 125.5 kPa.

For \(p = h \rho g\) questions, check whether the question asks for pressure from the liquid only or total pressure (which includes atmospheric pressure).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with container walls; increasing temperature or decreasing volume increases pressure.
  • Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and is calculated using \(p = h \rho g\).
  • Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude; upthrust is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of a submerged object.

lessons.title: Nuclear Radiation: Uses, Fission and Fusion
lessons.description: How nuclear fission and fusion release energy and how radiation is used.
lessons.content_html:
Nuclear Fission

Nuclear fission is the splitting of a large, unstable nucleus into two smaller daughter nuclei. This process releases a large amount of energy, along with two or three neutrons and gamma radiation. Fission can occur spontaneously in very unstable isotopes, but in nuclear reactors it is induced by bombarding a fissile nucleus (such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239) with a slow-moving neutron.

When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, it becomes unstable and splits. The two daughter nuclei and the released neutrons carry away kinetic energy. The total mass of the products is slightly less than the mass of the original nucleus plus the neutron — this “missing” mass has been converted into energy according to Einstein’s equation \(E = mc^2\).

Key Fact

In nuclear fission, the neutrons released can go on to cause further fission events. If at least one neutron from each fission causes another fission, a self-sustaining chain reaction occurs.

In a nuclear power station, the chain reaction must be controlled so that exactly one neutron from each fission event causes another fission. Control rods (made of boron or cadmium) absorb excess neutrons. Lowering the rods into the reactor core slows the reaction; raising them speeds it up.

A moderator (usually water or graphite) slows down fast-moving neutrons. Slow neutrons are more likely to be absorbed by uranium-235 nuclei, making fission more likely. The energy from fission heats a coolant (often water), which produces steam to drive turbines connected to generators, producing electricity.

Nuclear Fusion

Nuclear fusion is the process where two light nuclei join together to form a larger nucleus. This releases a huge amount of energy — even more per kilogram than fission. Fusion is the process that powers stars, including our Sun. In the Sun’s core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium at temperatures of around 15 million °C.

Fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth because the nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. To overcome this electrostatic repulsion, extremely high temperatures and pressures are needed to force the nuclei close enough together for the strong nuclear force to take over and bind them. Maintaining these conditions long enough to sustain a fusion reaction is a major engineering challenge.

Key Fact

Both fission and fusion release energy because the products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the reactants. The “missing” mass is converted to energy via \(E = mc^2\).

Fission splits large nuclei (like uranium-235) and is used in current nuclear power stations. It produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely for thousands of years. Fusion joins small nuclei (like hydrogen isotopes) and produces far less radioactive waste. However, no commercially viable fusion reactor exists yet because of the extreme conditions required.

Both processes convert a small amount of mass into a large amount of energy. Fusion releases more energy per kilogram of fuel and uses hydrogen (abundant in seawater) as fuel, making it a potentially clean and almost unlimited energy source for the future.

Uses of Nuclear Radiation

Nuclear radiation has many practical applications beyond power generation. In medicine, gamma rays are used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells. A focused beam of gamma radiation is aimed at a tumour from multiple angles, concentrating the dose on the cancer while minimising damage to healthy tissue. Radioactive tracers (such as technetium-99m) are injected into the body and tracked using a gamma camera to diagnose conditions like blocked blood vessels or organ function problems.

In industry, beta or gamma sources are used to monitor the thickness of materials during manufacturing. If the material gets too thick, less radiation passes through to the detector, triggering an adjustment. Gamma radiation is also used to sterilise medical equipment and food, killing bacteria without chemicals or heat.

The choice of radiation type depends on its penetrating power and ionising ability. Alpha particles are highly ionising but have very low penetration — they are stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. They are used in smoke detectors, where alpha particles ionise air between two electrodes. When smoke enters, it absorbs the alpha particles, the current drops, and the alarm sounds.

Beta particles penetrate further (stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium) and are used for thickness monitoring of thin materials like paper or aluminium foil. Gamma rays are the most penetrating (only significantly reduced by thick lead or concrete) and are chosen for sterilisation and medical imaging because they can pass through the body.

Nuclear Waste and Safety

Nuclear fission produces radioactive waste, which is categorised as low-level, intermediate-level or high-level depending on its activity and half-life. Low-level waste (contaminated clothing, tools) is compacted and stored in lined, shallow trenches. Intermediate-level waste is mixed with concrete and stored in steel containers. High-level waste (spent fuel rods) generates significant heat and must be cooled before being vitrified (turned into glass) and stored deep underground in geological repositories.

Safety precautions when handling radioactive materials include: keeping exposure time as short as possible, maintaining maximum distance from the source, using appropriate shielding (lead-lined containers, thick concrete walls), and monitoring exposure with film badges or electronic dosimeters.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When comparing fission and fusion, make sure you clearly state which involves splitting and which involves joining. A common mistake is confusing the two. For questions about nuclear reactors, name the function of each component (control rods, moderator, coolant) separately — do not merge their roles.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nuclear fission splits large unstable nuclei, releasing energy and neutrons that sustain a chain reaction; reactors use control rods and moderators to manage this.
  • Nuclear fusion joins small nuclei at extreme temperatures and pressures, releasing even more energy per kilogram than fission; it powers stars but is not yet viable on Earth.
  • Nuclear radiation is used in medicine (radiotherapy, tracers), industry (thickness monitoring, sterilisation) and the home (smoke detectors), with the type chosen based on penetrating power.
